NAVIGATING THE WATER-ENERGY-FOOD NEXUS: ENVIRONMENTAL AND ECONOMIC FOOTPRINTS OF IRRIGATION TECHNOLOGIES IN JORDAN

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Motasem Darwish
Print ISSN : 2523-5664

ABSTRACT

Due to the arid climate and scarcity of water, Jordan faces many agricultural challenges. This research analyzes various irrigation methods, their economic performance, and environmental impacts in Jordan Valley (JV) and the Highlands (HL). In the JV, surface irrigation uses approximately 27.55 million cubic meters (mcm) of water every year, sourced from surface water, treated wastewater, and groundwater. This approach requires around 0.12 GWh of energy. Winter vegetables are the most efficient, yielding a water productivity of 10.65 kg/m³ and a net profit of 2.65 Jordanian Dinars (JD)/m³, and olives can produce only 0.17 JD/m³, showing a hard time in the economic life. On the other hand, HL mainly uses drip irrigation systems, approximately 274 mcm of water plus 229 GWh of energy are consumed. This territory also consumes approximately 40,770 tons of fertilizers, leading to issues with soil health and environmental sustainability. Taken together, the irrigation water expenditure in Jordan is 560 mcm, energy consumption is approximately 260 GWh and fertilizer application is 78,808 tons. The results highlighted the pressing demand of utilizing water and nutrient-efficient irrigation techniques with the least damage to the environment, enabling agricultural sustainability and food security in the face of water shortages and climate change.
